subject: anatomy
title: First Arch Malformations and Treacher Collins Syndrome

steps.tx: Malformations of the head and neck frequently reflect abnormal proliferation, migration, or survival of cranial neural crest cells supplying the branchial arches. The prototype first pharyngeal arch malformation is **Treacher Collins syndrome**, or mandibulofacial dysostosis, transmitted in an autosomal dominant pattern with variable expressivity due to mutations in the TCOF1 gene.
steps.say: Congenital head and neck anomalies often stem from failed neural crest migration into branchial arches. The classical first arch disorder is Treacher Collins syndrome, or mandibulofacial dysostosis, an autosomal dominant condition linked to TCOF1 mutations.

vis.alt: First and second pharyngeal arch derivatives and skeletal elements
vis.caption: First and second pharyngeal arch skeletal components involved in dysostosis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Treacher Collins syndrome results from extensive neural crest cell apoptosis during early organogenesis, crippling development of both the maxillary and mandibular prominences of the first arch and the second arch. Patients exhibit downward-slanting palpebral fissures, coloboma of the lower eyelids, malar hypoplasia from absent or underdeveloped **zygomatic bones**, and mandibular micrognathia.
steps.say: Treacher Collins syndrome arises from neural crest apoptosis that cripples first and second arch derivatives. Clinical signs include antimongoloid palpebral slanting, lower eyelid colobomas, malar flattening from hypoplastic zygomatic arches, and micrognathia.

right.title: Soft Tissue and Sensory Defects
points: Coloboma of the lateral third of lower eyelid
Microtia, atresia of external auditory canal
Conductive hearing loss from ossicular hypoplasia

steps.tx: Auditory defects in Treacher Collins syndrome stem from malformation of the first cleft, first arch, and second arch elements. The external ear displays microtia or anotia with atresia of the external auditory canal. Malformed malleus, incus, and stapes cause severe **conductive hearing loss**, although inner ear sensorineural hearing is spared because the otic vesicle develops independently.
steps.say: Auditory impairment in Treacher Collins stems from flawed first cleft, first arch, and second arch development. External microtia and canal atresia combine with deformed middle ear ossicles to cause conductive deafness, while inner ear cochlear function is preserved.

nodes.label: First and Second Arch Skeletal Failure

steps.tx: Another classic first arch developmental spectrum is the **Pierre Robin sequence**, initiated by primary micrognathia. Severe mandibular hypoplasia prevents the developing tongue from descending into the oral cavity. The abnormally positioned, retroplaced tongue (glossoptosis) physically prevents horizontal palatal shelf fusion, producing a wide U-shaped cleft palate.
steps.say: Another major first arch condition is the Pierre Robin sequence, triggered by primary micrognathia. A tiny mandible prevents the tongue from descending, causing glossoptosis that blocks palatal shelves from fusing, resulting in a U-shaped cleft palate.

nodes.label: U-Shaped Cleft Palate and Airway Stridor

steps.tx: In contrast to first arch dysostoses, **DiGeorge syndrome** is a neurocristopathy affecting the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, caused by a 22q11.2 microdeletion. Disruption of neural crest signaling cripples development of the thymus and parathyroid glands, presenting with severe T-cell immunodeficiency, neonatal hypocalcemic tetany, and conotruncal cardiac defects.
steps.say: Unlike first arch syndromes, DiGeorge syndrome stems from defective third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development caused by a 22q11.2 microdeletion. Crest migration failure impairs the thymus and parathyroids, causing T-cell immunodeficiency, hypocalcemia, and conotruncal heart defects.

vis.alt: Agenesis of third and fourth pharyngeal pouches in DiGeorge syndrome
vis.caption: Third and fourth pharyngeal pouch agenesis in DiGeorge neurocristopathy. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The clinical presentation of DiGeorge syndrome is recalled by the mnemonic CATCH-22: Cardiac anomalies (tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch), Abnormal facies, **Thymic hypoplasia** with T-cell deficiency, Cleft palate, and Hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid aplasia. Cardiac outflow defects stem directly from failure of neural crest cells to septate the truncus arteriosus.
steps.say: DiGeorge syndrome features the classic CATCH-22 pentad: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, and Hypocalcemia. Aorticopulmonary septal failure causes conotruncal cardiac malformations like tetralogy of Fallot.

rows: Absent T cells, recurrent fungal/viral infection

steps.tx: A unilateral first and second arch anomaly is **hemifacial microsomia**, or oculoauriculovertebral spectrum (Goldenhar syndrome). Characterized by asymmetrical hypoplasia of the mandible, maxilla, and ear on one side, it is accompanied by preauricular skin tags, epibulbar dermoids on the eye, and vertebral segmentation defects like hemivertebrae.
steps.say: An asymmetrical first and second arch defect is hemifacial microsomia, seen in Goldenhar syndrome. Marked by unilateral facial bone and ear hypoplasia, it features preauricular skin tags, epibulbar dermoids, and cervical hemivertebrae.

left.title: Treacher Collins Syndrome
points: Spares vertebral column and internal organs

steps.tx: Surgical management of first arch anomalies requires multidisciplinary staging: neonatal mandibular distraction osteogenesis relieves tongue-base airway obstruction in Pierre Robin sequence, while custom rib grafts or distraction reconstruct hypoplastic zygomatic arches and mandibles in Treacher Collins. In DiGeorge syndrome, **thymic transplantation** or HLA-matched bone marrow rescue immune competence.
steps.say: Management of first arch disorders demands staged intervention: neonatal mandibular distraction relieves airway obstruction in Pierre Robin, while bone grafts reconstruct the facial skeleton in Treacher Collins. In complete DiGeorge syndrome, thymic transplantation restores immune function.
